nodes.title: Markets, demand and customer orientation

teaching_content.core_explanation: A market is the setting in which actual and potential buyers and sellers interact around a customer need, product category or solution. Demand is the quantity customers are willing and able to buy under particular conditions; it is not the same as simply wanting a product. Customer orientation means using evidence about customer needs, behaviour and experience to shape what the business offers and how it operates. It does not mean accepting every customer request or assuming customers can always articulate the best solution. Marketing therefore begins with understanding customers and markets and extends through value propositions, pricing, communication, channels, service and relationships. A useful customer-journey view considers how people become aware of an offer, evaluate it, buy, experience the product/service, decide whether to remain, and potentially advocate for it. These stages are an analytical model rather than a universal sequence. Customer relationship management (CRM) combines processes, people and data to manage interactions and support acquisition, service, retention and development of customer relationships. CRM is not just software: poor data, weak service processes or misaligned incentives can make an expensive CRM system ineffective.
teaching_content.why_it_matters: Marketing decisions only make sense relative to the market, customer need and organisation's ability to deliver value. The node also links marketing promises to operations, data and long-term customer relationships.
definitions: market: arena in which buyers and sellers interact around a need or category
demand: willingness and ability to purchase at given conditions
customer orientation: systematic use of customer evidence to guide value creation
customer journey: model of customer interactions from awareness through purchase/use/retention/advocacy
CRM: coordinated use of processes, people and information to manage customer relationships
important_boundaries: customer orientation is not the same as doing everything customers ask
demand requires ability as well as willingness to buy
CRM is not merely a software database
customer satisfaction is not identical to loyalty
a customer journey is a model, not a fixed law
facts: customer needs and willingness to pay vary across segments and contexts
marketing and operations jointly create the customer experience
customer data can improve decisions but can also be incomplete, biased or constrained by privacy expectations
mechanisms: better understanding of customer problems -> stronger value proposition -> improved conversion/retention
poor delivery/service -> negative experience -> complaints/churn/reputation effects
CRM data -> more relevant targeting/service -> possible retention or cross-sell benefits if data and execution are sound
causal_relationships: customer need -> proposition -> marketing promise -> operational delivery -> experience -> retention/advocacy
poor experience -> complaint/review -> brand effect -> future demand
better relationship data -> more targeted action -> response -> updated data
examples: A subscription business can improve retention by identifying the point in the customer journey where new users fail to achieve first value, then redesigning onboarding rather than merely increasing advertising.
A premium retailer that advertises personalised service but understaffs stores creates inconsistency between marketing promise and operational delivery.
non_examples: Calling advertising 'marketing' as if pricing, customer research, service and channels were separate.
Installing a CRM platform without changing customer-service processes and assuming customer relationships will improve automatically.
applications: map an unfamiliar business's customer journey
identify where marketing and operations jointly determine experience
evaluate whether CRM use solves a real customer or decision problem
real_world_transfer: Diagnose why a business with strong awareness still has weak repeat purchase.
Identify whether a customer metric measures satisfaction, loyalty, recommendation or something else.
assumptions: Journey stages and CRM practices vary by product, buying process and channel.
limitations: Customer data describes observed behaviour imperfectly and can create false precision; not all retention is desirable if customers are unprofitable or strategically misaligned.

misconceptions.correction: Promotion is one part of marketing; marketing includes understanding markets/customers, proposition, pricing, channels and relationships.

misconceptions.incorrect_belief: CRM is a piece of software.
misconceptions.correction: Software can support CRM, but effective relationship management also depends on data quality, processes, people, service and objectives.

interpretation: customer metrics require definition and causal caution
common_errors: treating satisfaction or recommendation measures as direct proof of future sales

models_frameworks: customer journey as a useful teaching/analytical model
evidence_of_understanding: map and critique a customer journey
evaluate CRM as a process rather than technology alone

nodes.title: Market size, market growth and market share

teaching_content.core_explanation: Market size measures the total sales in a defined market over a period, normally by value or volume. Market growth measures how that total changes over time. Market share measures a particular firm's sales as a proportion of the defined market. Every one of these measures depends on definition: geography, product boundary, time period, customer type, currency and whether sales are measured by value or volume. A business can increase sales while losing market share if the market grows faster; it can gain share while sales fall if the market contracts more quickly. Market share is therefore an indicator of relative position, not proof of profitability, cash generation, customer loyalty or durable competitive advantage. Strong analysis asks what changed in the numerator and denominator and why.
teaching_content.why_it_matters: These are core marketing measures used to assess opportunity and relative performance, but they are frequently misinterpreted when market definition or the denominator is ignored.
definitions: market size: total sales in a defined market over a stated period
market growth: percentage change in total market size
market share: firm's sales divided by total market sales
value market share: share measured in monetary sales
volume market share: share measured in units/quantity
important_boundaries: market share is not market size
sales growth is not automatically share growth
value share and volume share can move differently
share does not prove profitability or competitive advantage
facts: market definitions can materially alter reported share
inflation can increase nominal market value without equivalent real volume growth
a shrinking market can produce rising share for a business whose sales are still falling
mechanisms: firm sales change relative to market total -> share changes
price/mix changes can raise value share without raising volume share
new entrants or category redefinition can change the market denominator
causal_relationships: market demand/price mix -> market size -> growth opportunity
firm growth rate relative to market -> change in market share
examples: A business sells £12m in a £120m market: share = 10%. The next year sales rise to £13m but the market reaches £145m: share falls to about 9.0%. Sales grew, relative share fell.
non_examples: Claiming a firm is more profitable because its market share increased.
Comparing market shares calculated from different market definitions.
applications: test how market definition changes the conclusion
separate sales performance from relative competitive position
real_world_transfer: Question whether a reported share increase reflects genuine competitive progress or simply market contraction/definition changes.
assumptions: The firm's sales and total market data are measured consistently.
limitations: Market data can be estimated; boundaries may be contestable; share can ignore profitability, customer quality and future disruption.

misconceptions.incorrect_belief: If sales rise, market share rises.
misconceptions.correction: Share rises only if the firm's sales grow faster than the defined market total.

misconceptions.incorrect_belief: High market share means high profit.
misconceptions.correction: Profit also depends on price, cost, mix, investment and many other factors.

methods.name: Market share
methods.interpretation: The firm accounts for 10% of sales under the stated market definition.

methods.name: Market growth
methods.formula: (new market size - old market size) / old market size × 100
methods.interpretation: The defined market grew by about 20.8% in nominal value.

worked_examples: A firm's sales rise from £12m to £13m while the market grows from £120m to £145m. Share falls from 10% to about 8.97%.
interpretation: Always compare firm growth with market growth and state the market definition.
common_errors: using the firm's sales as the denominator

evidence_of_understanding: challenge invalid conclusions from share data

nodes.title: Market research

teaching_content.core_explanation: Market research is the systematic collection and interpretation of information to reduce uncertainty about customers, competitors, markets or marketing decisions. Good research begins with a decision question, not with a preferred method. Primary research generates new evidence for the current problem; secondary research uses existing evidence. Quantitative evidence helps estimate magnitude, frequency or relationships; qualitative evidence helps explore motivations, experiences and mechanisms. Neither is inherently superior. A large transactional dataset can be precise about what happened but weak at explaining why; interviews can expose important reasons but may not estimate how widespread those reasons are. Strong research therefore considers relevance, validity, reliability, sampling, recency, bias, cost, ethics and triangulation. Research reduces uncertainty; it does not remove it, and evidence should be interpreted as conditional rather than converted into false certainty.
teaching_content.why_it_matters: Marketing and strategic decisions are frequently made under uncertainty. Research quality determines whether data genuinely improves the decision or merely gives a numerical appearance of confidence.
definitions: primary research: evidence collected specifically for the current question
secondary research: existing evidence collected previously
quantitative data: numerical evidence about amount, frequency or relationship
qualitative data: non-numerical evidence about meaning, experience or mechanism
validity: extent to which evidence measures or answers what it is intended to
reliability: consistency of measurement or method
important_boundaries: primary is not automatically better than secondary
quantitative is not automatically objective
qualitative evidence is not merely anecdotal when gathered systematically
research findings are evidence, not guaranteed outcomes
facts: method choice should follow the research question
triangulating sources can reduce dependence on one method's weaknesses
existing business/customer data can be useful but may reflect historical customers rather than future target markets
mechanisms: clear decision question -> appropriate evidence -> reduced uncertainty -> improved choice
poor question wording/selection -> biased responses -> misleading conclusion
combining behavioural and attitudinal evidence -> stronger diagnosis
causal_relationships: research design -> evidence quality -> decision quality
bias/confounding -> misleading inference -> poor marketing decision
examples: A retailer sees churn rise. Transaction data identifies when customers leave; interviews reveal that delivery uncertainty, not price, is driving departures. The two methods answer different parts of the problem.
non_examples: Surveying social-media followers because they are convenient and describing the result as representative of all potential customers.
Treating a correlation in sales data as proof of causation.
applications: choose and justify primary/secondary and qualitative/quantitative methods
real_world_transfer: Challenge market research whose sample cannot represent the intended market.
Distinguish evidence about customer behaviour from evidence about the causes of that behaviour.
assumptions: Research is only useful if the decision can respond to what is learned and the data collection is ethical/feasible.
limitations: Preferences and markets change; stated intentions can differ from behaviour; small qualitative samples are not designed to estimate prevalence.

misconceptions.incorrect_belief: Primary research is more reliable because it is new.
misconceptions.correction: Reliability depends on design and execution; high-quality secondary data can be superior to poor primary research.

misconceptions.incorrect_belief: Big data removes the need for judgement.
misconceptions.correction: Large datasets can still be biased, incomplete or causally ambiguous.

evidence_of_understanding: explain why mixed evidence can improve a decision

nodes.title: Sampling, bias, representativeness and confidence

teaching_content.core_explanation: A sample is a subset of a population used to learn about the wider group. Sampling quality depends on how the sample is selected as well as its size. Random sampling gives members a known chance of selection; stratified sampling deliberately reflects relevant population subgroups; quota sampling fills predetermined categories without necessarily selecting randomly within them; convenience sampling uses accessible respondents and can be heavily biased. Sampling error is random variation between a sample estimate and the population value; increasing a well-selected sample can reduce this error. Sampling bias is systematic over- or under-representation caused by the selection process and is not cured simply by making the same biased sample larger. Confidence intervals provide a bounded way to communicate sampling uncertainty around an estimate under stated assumptions. At A-level Business, the key understanding is conceptual: an estimate is not exact, a narrower interval generally indicates greater precision under the same method, and an interval does not remove non-sampling bias or prove the underlying question was valid.
teaching_content.why_it_matters: Businesses often make claims from surveys. Learners need to tell whether those claims are representative and understand why a huge sample can still be wrong.
definitions: population: full group of interest
sample: subset observed
representativeness: degree to which the sample reflects relevant characteristics of the target population
sampling error: random difference caused by observing a sample rather than everyone
sampling bias: systematic distortion caused by selection/non-response/design
confidence interval: range used to express uncertainty around an estimate under specified statistical assumptions
important_boundaries: large sample size does not remove systematic bias
random sampling is not the same as casually choosing people at random
confidence intervals address sampling uncertainty, not every form of error
representativeness depends on the target population and decision
facts: non-response can bias a sample
question wording can create measurement bias even with a representative sample
subgroups can be missed if the sampling frame is incomplete
mechanisms: poor sampling frame -> systematic exclusion -> biased estimate
larger appropriately selected sample -> lower random sampling uncertainty
stratification -> better representation of important subgroups when designed correctly
causal_relationships: sample design -> evidence quality -> estimate uncertainty/bias -> marketing conclusion
examples: An online-only survey of a retailer's email subscribers may contain thousands of responses but exclude non-digital or disengaged customers. The size does not make it representative.
non_examples: Saying '5,000 people answered, so the survey must be reliable.'
Interpreting a 95% confidence interval as meaning there is a 95% probability that this particular calculated interval contains the true value without regard to the statistical procedure.
real_world_transfer: Challenge headline survey results that omit how respondents were selected.
Explain why a narrow confidence interval does not rescue a badly biased sampling frame.
assumptions: Confidence statements rely on the assumptions of the sampling procedure and measurement design.
limitations: Representativeness is multidimensional; businesses may not know the exact population composition; advanced inferential mathematics is beyond the common subject foundation unless a course requires it.

misconceptions.incorrect_belief: A bigger sample is always better.
misconceptions.correction: A bigger biased sample can provide a more precise estimate of the wrong population.

misconceptions.incorrect_belief: A confidence interval captures all uncertainty.
misconceptions.correction: It does not automatically account for selection bias, poor wording, measurement error or future market change.

methods: conceptual interpretation of confidence intervals; exact calculation is course-dependent
worked_examples: If two otherwise comparable surveys estimate the same proportion but one has a materially wider confidence interval, the wider interval signals less sampling precision; neither interval proves the sample was unbiased.
interpretation: precision and bias are separate questions
common_errors: treating an interval as a guarantee

uncertainties: Exact confidence-interval mathematical depth is course-specific.

teaching_content.core_explanation: Segmentation divides a broad market into groups whose needs, behaviours or responses differ in ways that are useful for decision making. Targeting is the choice of which segment or segments the business will prioritise. Positioning is the intended place of the offer in customers' minds relative to alternatives, supported by a coherent value proposition. The sequence matters: a business should not choose communications or product features before knowing who it is trying to serve and which customer problem it intends to solve. Segments can be based on demographic, geographic, behavioural, psychographic, income, usage or other relevant characteristics, but a descriptive category is only useful if it predicts a meaningful difference in needs or response. Target markets can be broad or niche; neither is inherently superior. Positioning must be credible and operationally deliverable. A premium positioning supported only by premium advertising but contradicted by poor service, distribution or quality is unstable. Market maps can help visualise perceived positions on selected dimensions, but the chosen axes are subjective and may omit what customers actually value.
teaching_content.why_it_matters: STP links market understanding to coherent product, price, channel, promotion and operations decisions.
definitions: segmentation: dividing a market into meaningful groups
targeting: selecting segment(s) to prioritise
positioning: intended relative perception of the offering
niche market: narrower specialised target
mass market: broad market serving large customer groups
market map: visual representation of perceived positions on selected dimensions
important_boundaries: a demographic group is not automatically a useful segment
positioning is not just a slogan
niche does not automatically mean small profit or premium price
market maps depend on chosen dimensions and perceptions
facts: effective segments should be identifiable and useful for differentiated action
targeting decisions depend on attractiveness and organisational capability
positioning must be reinforced by the wider marketing mix and delivery system
mechanisms: segmentation -> more relevant proposition/action -> improved response where differences are real
clear position -> reduced customer uncertainty/differentiation -> possible pricing/choice effects
poor fit between target and capability -> disappointing experience -> weak retention
causal_relationships: customer heterogeneity -> segmentation -> target choice -> proposition/position -> marketing mix/operations
position promise -> actual experience -> reinforcement or erosion of position
examples: A gym may target time-poor professionals with 24-hour access and short guided sessions; the target affects service design and location, not only advertising.
non_examples: Defining '18-25 year olds' as a segment without evidence they share relevant needs.
Calling a logo redesign 'repositioning' when product, price and service are unchanged.
applications: assess whether the marketing mix supports the intended position
real_world_transfer: Explain why two customers of the same age can belong to different useful behavioural segments.
Identify an operational inconsistency that undermines positioning.
assumptions: Customer preferences can be meaningfully grouped and observed.
limitations: Segments can overlap/change; excessive segmentation raises complexity; market maps simplify multi-dimensional perceptions.

misconceptions.incorrect_belief: Segmentation means dividing customers by age or income.
misconceptions.correction: Those are possible variables; useful segmentation is any grouping that predicts material differences in needs/behaviour and supports action.

misconceptions.incorrect_belief: Positioning is what the business says about itself.
misconceptions.correction: Positioning concerns customer perception relative to alternatives and must be supported by actual delivery.

nodes.title: Product, service, value proposition and product-life-cycle thinking

teaching_content.core_explanation: A product or service is a bundle of functional benefits, experiences, meanings and supporting services offered to solve a customer problem. The value proposition explains why a target customer should prefer that offer to available alternatives. Product decisions include features, quality, design, range, service, packaging, support, portfolio role and innovation. Product-life-cycle thinking describes a possible pattern in which sales move through introduction, growth, maturity and decline. It can help managers ask how awareness, competition, investment, pricing, capacity and promotional priorities might change as a category evolves. It is not a deterministic law or timetable. Products can be repositioned, extended, relaunched, moved into new markets or disrupted suddenly; different segments can be at different stages. Extension strategies therefore aim to alter demand or relevance rather than magically reset a fixed biological cycle. Product portfolio tools such as the BCG matrix are separate analytical frameworks and should not be treated as proof of what to do with a product.
teaching_content.why_it_matters: Product decisions determine what value is actually delivered and connect marketing to operations, innovation, finance and strategy.
definitions: product/service: offering designed to create customer value
value proposition: reason a target customer should choose the offer
product portfolio: collection of products/brands managed by a business
product life cycle: teaching model describing possible sales evolution through introduction, growth, maturity and decline
extension strategy: action intended to prolong/revive demand or relevance
important_boundaries: product is more than physical features
PLC stages are not inevitable
maturity is an interpretation of evidence, not a certainty
a new feature is not automatically innovation that creates value
facts: services often depend heavily on process and people
portfolio products can share brand, channels or resources
life-cycle patterns differ by market and can be disrupted
mechanisms: better product-market fit -> stronger customer response -> sales/retention
quality/design change -> cost/experience -> positioning/margin effect
extension action -> altered customer/market relevance -> possible change in sales trajectory
causal_relationships: customer problem -> value proposition -> product/service design -> experience -> demand/retention
portfolio decision -> shared resource/cannibalisation -> financial/strategic outcome
examples: A streaming service can extend a mature domestic offer by entering new geographic markets or bundling new content; this does not prove the original market has returned to an 'introduction' stage.
non_examples: Predicting sales decline solely because a product has existed for many years.
Describing cosmetic packaging changes as successful product development without customer or commercial evidence.
real_world_transfer: Recognise when a manager is treating a lifecycle diagram as destiny rather than a hypothesis.
Explain why a service's process and people can be part of the product experience.
assumptions: Life-cycle use assumes meaningful sales/history data and reasonably defined market/category.
limitations: Lifecycle stages can be ambiguous and retrospective; aggregation can hide segment differences.

misconceptions.incorrect_belief: All products move through the same four stages in order.
misconceptions.correction: The lifecycle is a model for thinking about possible patterns, not a universal law.

misconceptions.incorrect_belief: A product is just the physical item.
misconceptions.correction: Customer value may depend on service, support, convenience, brand and experience as well as physical features.

interpretation: sales trends can inform but not determine lifecycle interpretation

teaching_content.core_explanation: A brand is the set of identifiers, expectations, associations and experiences that customers connect with an organisation, product or service. Logos, names and visual identity are brand assets but do not by themselves create a strong brand. Differentiation means creating a meaningful reason for customers to perceive the offering as distinct from alternatives. Brand equity is the economic and strategic value associated with brand recognition, trust, loyalty, perceived quality or other customer responses. Strong brands can lower perceived purchase risk, improve recognition, support customer retention or price premiums and make new-product introduction easier. But brand equity is earned through consistent delivery as well as communications. If service, quality or corporate behaviour repeatedly contradicts the promise, trust can fall quickly. Differentiation also creates costs: additional features, design, service or marketing only create value if target customers care enough and competitors cannot neutralise the distinction cheaply.
teaching_content.why_it_matters: Brand and differentiation connect customer perception to pricing power, loyalty, risk and competitive advantage, while showing why marketing claims must be supported operationally.
definitions: brand: network of identifiers, meanings, expectations and experiences attached to an offering/organisation
differentiation: meaningful distinction from alternatives
brand equity: value associated with brand-driven customer/market responses
brand loyalty: tendency to continue choosing a brand, which may arise from preference, habit, switching cost or other causes
important_boundaries: brand is not a logo
awareness is not loyalty
loyalty can reflect inertia rather than affection
differentiation must matter to the target customer
facts: brand reduces information/search costs for customers when it creates reliable expectations
operational inconsistency can damage brand trust
strong differentiation can make demand less price sensitive but not always
mechanisms: consistent positive experience -> trust/recognition -> lower perceived risk -> possible repeat purchase/premium
differentiated benefit -> reduced substitutability -> possible pricing power
brand failure/public controversy -> trust loss -> demand/retention/recruitment effects
causal_relationships: promise -> delivery -> experience -> associations/trust -> future demand
differentiation -> perceived substitutability -> elasticity/price effect
examples: A premium delivery brand that consistently meets narrow delivery windows can build trust; repeated missed slots can destroy the very differentiation the advertising claims.
non_examples: Assuming an expensive advertising campaign creates brand equity if the product experience is unchanged or poor.
applications: identify the actual source of differentiation
evaluate whether the brand promise is operationally credible
connect brand strength to elasticity and competitive advantage
real_world_transfer: Question whether reported 'loyalty' reflects true preference, contracts, convenience or switching costs.
Explain why a reputation problem can affect recruitment and supplier relationships as well as sales.
assumptions: Brand effects differ by purchase risk, involvement, substitutes and customer segment.
limitations: Brand equity is difficult to measure directly; awareness metrics can overstate economic value.

misconceptions.incorrect_belief: A brand is a name and logo.
misconceptions.correction: Those are identifiers; the brand also includes expectations, associations and experienced delivery.

misconceptions.incorrect_belief: High awareness means strong brand equity.
misconceptions.correction: People can know a brand and dislike, distrust or avoid it.

interpretation: brand metrics require distinction between awareness, preference, retention and economic value

nodes.title: Pricing, price elasticity, income elasticity and revenue effects

teaching_content.core_explanation: Price is both a source of revenue per unit and a signal that influences demand, positioning and customer expectations. Businesses can use cost-plus, competitor-informed, penetration, skimming, value-based, dynamic, psychological or other approaches; these are methods for informing a decision rather than universally correct rules. Price elasticity of demand (PED) measures how responsive quantity demanded is to a percentage change in price. Income elasticity of demand (YED) measures how responsive quantity demanded is to a percentage change in consumer income. PED is normally negative because price and quantity demanded tend to move in opposite directions; analysis usually focuses on its absolute magnitude. If absolute PED is above one, demand is relatively price elastic; below one, relatively price inelastic. YED can be positive for normal goods and negative for inferior goods; a higher positive value indicates greater responsiveness to income change. Elasticity is not fixed forever: it can change with time horizon, availability of substitutes, brand strength, customer segment, proportion of income spent and market conditions. A price change that increases revenue does not automatically increase profit because variable cost, contribution, capacity, brand and long-term customer behaviour also matter.
teaching_content.why_it_matters: Pricing decisions require a causal link from price/income to demand, revenue, contribution, operations and positioning. Elasticity gives a disciplined way to reason about responsiveness without pretending the number decides the strategy.
definitions: price elasticity of demand (PED): percentage change in quantity demanded divided by percentage change in price
income elasticity of demand (YED): percentage change in quantity demanded divided by percentage change in consumer income
price elastic demand: absolute PED greater than 1
price inelastic demand: absolute PED less than 1
normal good: demand generally rises as income rises, positive YED
inferior good: demand generally falls as income rises, negative YED
important_boundaries: inelastic does not mean demand does not change
revenue effect is not profit effect
PED and YED answer different questions
elasticity estimates describe a range/context and can change
dynamic pricing still operates within consumer-protection/transparency constraints
facts: availability of substitutes usually affects price responsiveness
time can allow customers to find substitutes
income sensitivity differs across categories/segments
pricing changes can affect brand positioning and operational volume
mechanisms: price change -> quantity response -> revenue -> contribution/capacity/brand effects
income change -> category/segment demand response -> sales forecast -> capacity/inventory/workforce implications
differentiation -> reduced substitutability -> potentially lower price sensitivity
causal_relationships: price -> demand -> volume -> revenue/contribution -> capacity/cash
income -> demand by YED -> revenue/planning
branding/substitutes/time -> elasticity -> pricing consequences
examples: If price rises 10% and quantity demanded falls 4%, PED = -0.4. Demand is relatively inelastic over that change and revenue may rise, but profit still depends on contribution, costs and long-term effects.

If household income rises 5% and demand for a premium leisure service rises 10%, YED = +2.0, suggesting income-elastic demand in the observed context. A downturn could therefore create disproportionately large demand risk.
non_examples: Saying inelastic demand means quantity never falls when price rises.
Using a positive YED estimate to claim the product will always grow when the economy grows.
applications: trace a price decision into operations and finance
use income sensitivity in scenario planning
real_world_transfer: Explain why a business may reject a price increase even when historic PED suggests revenue would rise.
Identify categories likely to be more exposed to income downturns and explain planning implications.
assumptions: Elasticity estimates assume other important conditions are sufficiently comparable; observed changes can contain confounding effects.
limitations: Historic elasticity may not transfer to large price changes, new segments, competitor reactions or structural shocks.

misconceptions.incorrect_belief: If demand is inelastic, raising price always raises profit.
misconceptions.correction: It may raise revenue over the observed range, but profit depends on costs, volume, capacity, brand and longer-term response.

misconceptions.incorrect_belief: PED and YED are interchangeable measures of demand sensitivity.
misconceptions.correction: PED concerns price change; YED concerns consumer income change.

methods.name: PED
methods.formula: % change in quantity demanded / % change in price
methods.interpretation: Demand is relatively price inelastic over the observed change.

methods.name: YED
methods.formula: % change in quantity demanded / % change in consumer income
methods.interpretation: Demand is positive and strongly responsive to income in the observed context.

worked_examples: Price £20 -> £22 (+10%); quantity 1,000 -> 960 (-4%): PED -0.4. Revenue moves from £20,000 to £21,120, but the profit conclusion still requires unit costs and wider effects.
interpretation: Magnitude and sign must be interpreted in context; elasticity is evidence for a decision, not the decision.
common_errors: using absolute quantity change instead of percentage change

uncertainties: Exact calculation versus interpretation requirements vary by course and should be mapped explicitly.

nodes.title: Promotion, channels, digital marketing and the integrated marketing mix

teaching_content.core_explanation: Promotion communicates with customers and other audiences to inform, persuade, remind or maintain relationships. Distribution ('place') concerns how customers obtain the product/service and can affect reach, convenience, margin, control, data and service quality. Digital marketing changes targeting, measurement, interaction and channel economics but does not replace the need for a coherent proposition. The traditional four Ps—product, price, promotion and place—provide a simple decision checklist; the extended seven Ps add people, process and physical evidence, which are particularly useful when customer experience depends heavily on service delivery. The marketing mix should be integrated: a premium position supported by low-quality fulfilment, indiscriminate discounting and weak customer service is internally inconsistent. Channel choices also create operational and financial consequences: direct-to-consumer channels can provide customer data and margin but require fulfilment capability; intermediaries can expand reach but reduce control or margin. Digital metrics such as clicks and impressions measure activity, not automatically customer value or profit. Strong marketing evaluation therefore connects communication and channel choices to target customer behaviour, costs, capacity, customer experience and the wider strategy.
teaching_content.why_it_matters: This node turns marketing from a list of tactics into a coherent system of mutually reinforcing choices and links digital activity to real business outcomes.
definitions: promotion: communication activity intended to influence awareness, understanding or behaviour
channel of distribution: route through which customers access the offering
multi-channel: use of more than one route/channel
integrated marketing mix: coordinated product/price/promotion/place/people/process/physical-evidence decisions
digital marketing: use of digital channels/data/technology to reach and interact with audiences
important_boundaries: promotion is not the whole of marketing
digital activity metrics are not the same as commercial outcomes
direct channels are not automatically cheaper once fulfilment/service costs are included
an integrated mix requires consistency with target and positioning
facts: channels affect data access, margin and customer experience
promotion effectiveness depends on audience, message, medium, timing and objective
service businesses often depend heavily on people/process/physical evidence
mechanisms: promotion -> awareness/response -> traffic/conversion -> sales/relationship outcome
channel choice -> reach/control/margin/service -> customer experience and financial effect
digital data -> targeting/optimisation -> possible improved efficiency but also privacy/bias concerns
causal_relationships: target/position -> mix choices -> customer experience -> demand/retention
channel -> fulfilment requirements -> cost/capacity -> service quality
promotion volume -> demand spike -> operational load -> customer outcome
examples: A direct-to-consumer brand gains customer data and avoids wholesale margin but must finance warehouses, returns and customer service; the channel decision cannot be evaluated only by the selling margin.
non_examples: Judging a campaign successful because video views increased without linking views to the campaign objective.
Using heavy price promotion while claiming an exclusive premium position without explaining the strategic logic.
applications: trace campaign effects into operations and finance
real_world_transfer: Challenge a digital campaign report that celebrates clicks but gives no conversion, margin or retention evidence.
Explain why a successful promotion can still damage the business if operations cannot fulfil the demand.
assumptions: Attribution of outcomes to one marketing activity can be difficult because customers experience multiple influences.
limitations: The 4Ps/7Ps are useful checklists but do not create a strategy or establish causation; platform algorithms and privacy rules can change quickly.

misconceptions.correction: Response depends on relevance, audience, offer, competition, saturation and delivery capability.

misconceptions.incorrect_belief: Digital marketing is automatically cheaper and more measurable.
misconceptions.correction: Digital channels have bidding, content, technology and data costs; measurement can still suffer attribution and causality problems.

methods: campaign and channel performance measures are context-specific and should be linked to objectives
interpretation: activity measures such as impressions/clicks do not establish incremental profit

evidence_of_understanding: compare channels with full business consequences
